opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that the hardware has come a long way, but it's not yet where it needs to be for living side by side with people in a home.

If you look at something like Optimus, or a lot of the other humanoids people are building now, the progress in actuators, in degrees of freedom, in how cheaply you can manufacture these things, has been really impressive. A few years ago a capable humanoid was a research artifact that cost as much as a house. Now people are talking seriously about price points closer to a car. That's a big shift.

But when I think about the home specifically, there are a few things that still worry me. The first is safety. Most of these robots are fairly heavy and strong, and they're built with fairly rigid, high-gear-ratio actuation. That's great for precision and payload, but if something goes wrong near a child or an elderly person, the consequences can be serious. For the home, I think we really need hardware that is intrinsically safe: lighter, more compliant, maybe softer on the outside, so that even when the software makes a mistake, and it will, the physical outcome isn't dangerous.

The second is the hands. People underestimate how much of household work is really about manipulation: folding clothes, handling dishes, opening packaging, dealing with deformable and fragile objects. Current robot hands are still quite limited in robustness, in tactile sensing, and in durability. A hand that works beautifully in a demo might break after a few thousand grasps, and in a home you need it to work every day for years.

The third is reliability and maintenance. A factory has technicians. A home doesn't. So the hardware has to tolerate dust, spills, bumps, and people doing unexpected things around it, and keep running without someone recalibrating it every week.

And I'd add that I'm not totally convinced the humanoid form factor is always the right answer for the home. There's a good argument for it, since our homes are designed around human bodies, and it makes learning from human data more natural. But for many tasks, a simpler, lower, safer mobile manipulator might deliver more value sooner.

So overall, I'm optimistic. The trend is clearly in the right direction, and I think the intelligence side, the learning side, is now moving fast enough that hardware will become the bottleneck again. But to truly coexist with people at home, we need hardware designed from the start around safety, dexterity, and robustness, not just strength and impressive demos.

r002.rationale: It raises safety concerns around robots near people, but does not question whether they can stay stable after accidental physical disturbances.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll give you the honest version, which is that the hardware is further along than most people think and further from home-ready than the demo videos suggest.

Take Optimus as the clearest example. What Tesla has done well is treat the body as a manufacturing problem rather than a research artifact. The actuators are their own design, the hand has gone through several generations toward more degrees of freedom, and the whole thing is built with cost and volume in mind from day one. That matters, because a home robot only makes sense if it eventually costs something like a car, not a lab instrument. On that axis, Tesla is probably ahead of most of the field.

But working alongside people in a home is a very different bar from walking across a stage or sorting battery cells on a factory floor. Three things stand out to me.

First, safety at the physical level. A humanoid that weighs fifty or sixty kilos and can lift twenty is also a machine that can hurt a child or an elderly person if it falls or swings an arm at the wrong moment. Industrial robots solve this with cages and light curtains. A home has neither. So the hardware needs compliant actuation, good torque sensing in every joint, and a controller that fails gracefully when something unexpected happens. Most current humanoids, Optimus included, are still fairly stiff, high-gain systems. They're getting better, but I would not want one standing next to my grandmother yet.

Second, hands and touch. Folding laundry, loading a dishwasher, opening a jar: these are dominated by contact-rich manipulation, not by walking. Tesla's newer hand is a real step up, but tactile sensing across the fingertips and palm is still thin, and durability of those tendons and small actuators under thousands of daily cycles is an open question for everyone. The hand is where I'd bet most of the remaining hardware difficulty lives.

Third, the hardware-to-learning gap. The current approach everywhere is teleoperation data plus imitation learning, which is why so many demos are still a person in a VR headset. That's not cheating, it's how you bootstrap, but it means the hardware's real capability today is bounded by how much human demonstration you can collect. The home is unstructured in a way factories are not, so you need either enormous data or hardware that is forgiving enough that the policy's mistakes don't matter much. Right now we have neither in abundance.

So my assessment: for structured, repeatable tasks in a controlled environment, the hardware is close to good enough and we'll see real deployments within a couple of years. For the general home, I think we're looking at a few more hardware generations, mostly on hands, sensing, and intrinsic safety, before the body stops being the bottleneck and it becomes purely a software problem. And I'd say that about Optimus, Figure, Unitree, all of them. The differences between them are smaller than the distance any of them still has to go.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate an impressive demonstration from something you can comfortably live with. A home is an unpredictable environment: there are children, pets, objects on the floor, and people moving in ways the robot may not anticipate. The hardware needs to handle those situations safely, including when the software makes a mistake.

For something like Tesla Optimus, I’d look beyond whether it can perform a task once. Can it do it reliably, with appropriate force, and stop safely when someone gets in the way? How much supervision does it need? Those are more useful questions than how humanlike it looks.

My view is that the hardware is promising, but I’d be cautious about calling it ready for general household work. A robot that does a few useful tasks consistently would already be valuable. It doesn’t need to do everything, but people need to trust what it does.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate an impressive demonstration from a robot you can trust in your home. A demo shows that something is possible. Living alongside people means doing it reliably, day after day, around children, pets, clutter, and unexpected movement.

For systems like Tesla Optimus, I’d look closely at dexterity, force control, and how safely the robot handles mistakes. Can it pick up a delicate object without crushing it? Can it recognize when someone is in the way and stop safely? And how much human assistance does it need to complete a task?

My view is that the hardware is promising, but we shouldn’t equate a human-shaped body with readiness for household work. The useful first step is a limited set of tasks performed consistently and safely. That matters much more than how impressive the robot looks.
